selection: Thirty researched cases selected for organizational need, role fit and advanced-level evidence. Grouped by pathway, not ranked by debut probability; no league-rank cutoff.

coverage.pitchLevelMeasurements: Not independently collected. Specific weaknesses are attributed to dated scouting reports; proposed monitors are not claimed as measurements.

players.name: Ryan Sloan
players.why: His Double-A work makes a direct jump worth watching. Seattle already has six pitchers who made multiple MLB starts; a vacancy or a need for an extra starter is the realistic entry point.
players.opportunity: An injury, workload break or rotation change could create starts. Beating the next depth option matters more than his prospect rank; a full-time rotation place is not currently open.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports a glove-side location bias and a less consistent slider than splitter.
players.checkpoint: Command fastballs to the arm side, repeat the slider’s shape, and hold pitch quality deeper into starts.
players.monitor: Track arm-side target execution, slider consistency and late-start velocity; those pitch-level measurements have not been collected here.
players.need: Rotation coverage, not an unfilled everyday role. Six current options started MLB games, so opportunity depends on health, workload and depth ordering.

research.name: Ryan Sloan
research.assessment: The strongest part of his case is how often he gets ahead without giving away first base. That makes him more than a radar-gun prospect. The remaining starter test is whether hitters have to respect his whole mix after seeing him once; a low walk total by itself cannot show that the slider works deep into games.
research.firstRole: A spot start is the simpler route than an immediate permanent rotation place. Seattle could value his innings even while preferring an established starter over a full season.
checkpoints: A second reliable secondary pitch would make it harder to sit on his fastball.
Compare late-start execution with early innings before assuming he can hold the same quality through a full workload.

sourceUpdate.name: Ryan Sloan
sourceUpdate.finding: Seattle reported added two-seam and cutter looks, with late-count secondary command still a development goal.

players.name: Liam Doyle
players.why: A full Double-A starting workload gives him a route beyond his ranking. St. Louis used Pallante, Leahy, Liberatore and McGreevy for at least 29 starts each, with Mathews and Dobbins also starting.
players.opportunity: He must displace a rotation option or answer an injury need. A shorter bullpen assignment is another possible debut route, but would not mean he has passed the starter test.
players.observed: FanGraphs describes an overpowering fastball, but a slower breaker that can show early and draws little chase. Its report calls for a breaking-ball adjustment.
players.checkpoint: Make the breaker less recognizable out of the hand, command secondaries for strikes, and reduce walks while retaining a starter’s workload.
players.monitor: Follow breaking-ball chase and strike rates separately. The saved 2026 walk rate is a warning, not proof that a specific grip fix will work.
players.need: Potential rotation competition rather than a guaranteed vacancy. The incumbent group has a full season of starts; pitch execution must justify displacing someone.

research.name: Liam Doyle
research.assessment: Strikeouts show that the fastball can miss bats, but the walks make the route less straightforward than the draft pedigree suggests. If hitters can reject his breaker, he has to return to the fastball in predictable counts. Getting a secondary pitch over for a strike and getting chase with it are different tests; he needs evidence of both.
research.firstRole: A short relief look could arrive before a stable rotation assignment. That would demonstrate a narrower MLB use, while leaving the starting-pitcher question open.
checkpoints: Look for fewer hitter-friendly counts over consecutive starts, rather than one low-walk outing.
A better breaker must still work against hitters who have already seen the fastball.

sourceUpdate.name: Liam Doyle
sourceUpdate.finding: MLB described his initial Double-A assignment as aggressive; early struggles are context, not a current-season verdict.

players.name: Jamie Arnold
players.why: His season workload supports a starting path, but the tiny Triple-A sample and interrupted finish leave readiness unresolved. Recovery and normal preparation come before a rotation competition.
players.need: Several listed starters posted ERAs above 5.00, including Springs, Lopez, Perkins and Jump. That creates performance pressure rather than a promised vacancy.
players.opportunity: Outperform the next rotation option, with a depth assignment possible first. Other young pitchers also compete for the same innings.
players.observed: FanGraphs’ April report describes poor fastball strike/zone rates and falling behind, forcing heavy slider use to recover counts.
players.checkpoint: Confirm normal game preparation, then get fastball strikes earlier in counts and make the complementary pitch dependable.
players.monitor: Follow fastball strike rate and counts won early; the five-inning Triple-A ERA is not proof that the control problem is solved.

research.name: Jamie Arnold
research.assessment: The five-inning Triple-A line is an introduction, not a readiness verdict. His broader starting workload gives the pitching case substance, but the health interruption changes the order of the questions: first clearance and normal preparation, then strike throwing against advanced hitters. Earlier concerns about fastball location should be retested rather than assumed fixed by one scoreless outing.
research.firstRole: If healthy, rotation depth is a plausible first assignment. Without a verified recovery update, a spring roster place should remain conditional.
checkpoints: Confirm a normal throwing and fielding progression before interpreting spring results.
Watch whether fastball strikes create usable counts for the slider, instead of the slider constantly rescuing him.

sourceUpdate.name: Jamie Arnold
sourceUpdate.finding: Facial fractures interrupted his Triple-A arrival; no return timetable was announced.

players.name: Carlos Lagrange
players.why: His Triple-A experience puts him close enough for a depth call, but New York already has a substantial rotation group. The first MLB role could be shorter than the eventual development goal.
players.need: There are established options in both rotation and bullpen. Relief could create a narrower use than displacing a starter, but this is not an empty bullpen or a guaranteed high-leverage role.
players.opportunity: Earn useful short innings with repeatable strikes and dependable recovery between appearances. A future starting role would require a separate workload and command case.
players.observed: FanGraphs highlights elite velocity and multiple secondary options, but delivery effort and walks make relief a plausible outcome.
players.checkpoint: Repeat release timing and reduce free passes while retaining fastball quality and a dependable secondary strike.
players.monitor: Separate shorter-stint effectiveness from starter command; a relief debut would not mean the rotation questions were answered.

research.name: Carlos Lagrange
research.assessment: The first-role question is especially important here. A shorter assignment can let the fastball and best secondary play without requiring the same command and endurance as a start. Strong relief work would therefore support a call-up case, but it would not settle whether he can turn over a lineup or keep walks under control over longer outings.
research.firstRole: The announced relief experiment gives him a concrete route beyond waiting for a rotation vacancy. The club’s long-term starter view and his near-term bullpen use should be tracked separately.
checkpoints: Check strike throwing and recovery on a reliever’s schedule.
Evaluate changeup use and longer-outing execution separately if the club stretches him back out.

sourceUpdate.name: Carlos Lagrange
sourceUpdate.finding: New York announced a Triple-A relief move while retaining a longer-term starting goal.

players.name: Jack Wenninger
players.role: Rotation depth with a developed workload
players.why: A full Triple-A workload makes him a practical depth candidate even far outside the league’s top 100. His 2026 walks also show why an earlier positive report is not the same as present readiness.
players.need: Manaea posted a 4.78 ERA and Senga 7.34, while McLean, Scott and Thornton supply competition. Better depth has a plausible use.
players.opportunity: Win a spot-start or next-man-up assignment, then show he can hold it. The trade-value ranking does not decide the MLB depth ordering.
players.observed: FanGraphs sees a useful splitter and developed workload, but says too many breaking balls are flat, soft or backed up.
players.checkpoint: Make the breaker’s quality repeatable and restore better strike throwing, rather than leaning only on the splitter.
players.monitor: Track breaker execution and free passes; distinguish last season’s favorable control report from the higher saved 2026 walk rate.

research.name: Jack Wenninger
research.assessment: Triple-A volume makes him a practical next-man-up candidate, but the walk total weakens the claim that he is ready to hold a job. A good splitter can finish hitters only after he earns counts in which they must protect the zone. The useful question is whether the breaker and fastball let him reach those counts consistently.
research.firstRole: Spot starts or bulk coverage are more defensible than projecting an immediate regular rotation role. Sustained control improvement would make the assignment easier to retain.
checkpoints: Look for a repeatable breaker rather than occasional standout pitches.
Separate early-season scouting praise from what the later saved walk totals actually show.

sourceUpdate.name: Jack Wenninger
sourceUpdate.finding: MLB’s June Statcast review continued to identify the splitter as his best pitch.

players.name: Andrew Fischer
players.why: Third base is a more plausible route than first base: Milwaukee split third-base work among Hamilton, Ortiz and Vaughn. Fischer’s Double-A power puts him in that conversation despite a much lower league ranking.
players.opportunity: He has to win third-base work, not inherit an empty job. Moving to first or DH adds competition from Bauers, Vaughn, Yelich, Adams and Burke.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports swings over changeups, including pitches inside the zone, and hesitation on slow rollers.
players.checkpoint: Improve in-zone contact against changeups; make cleaner decisions on slow rollers at third.
players.monitor: Separate changeup contact from overall strikeouts. His Double-A strikeout rate is context, not a measured changeup-whiff rate.
players.need: A possible offensive upgrade at third: Hamilton posted a .650 OPS and Ortiz .730. Their defense still matters, and Fischer must earn the position.

research.name: Andrew Fischer
research.assessment: The power is already loud enough to deserve attention; the question is how much survives when pitchers can repeatedly target the contact weakness. Walks help, but they do not cancel empty swings on hittable changeups. Third-base competence matters because shifting to first would raise the offensive standard and place him in the same queue as Burke and Adams.
research.firstRole: A share of third-base work is the more useful first role than another first-base-only bat. He must offer enough offense and reliable defense to justify that choice.
checkpoints: Distinguish strike-zone changeup misses from chases outside the zone.
Routine slow-roller decisions matter alongside arm strength and highlight plays.

sourceUpdate.finding: MLB named him its Hitting Prospect of the Year after a 162 wRC+ season.

players.name: Luke Adams
players.why: His Triple-A sample and balanced strikeout/walk counts deserve attention even outside the top 100. First base is crowded; showing usable third-base defense would give him another way onto the roster.
players.opportunity: Vaughn already provides a right-handed first-base option. Adams needs an injury, transaction or a better all-around case; he and Burke cannot both be credited with the same hypothetical opening.
players.observed: FanGraphs questions whether modest contact impact and a walk/HBP-heavy approach clear the offensive bar at first base.
players.checkpoint: Turn hittable strikes into harder contact; preserve enough third-base defense to offer another route.
players.monitor: Watch damage on strikes and performance at third, rather than treating every walk or hit-by-pitch as proof of MLB readiness.
players.need: No obvious first-base production hole: Vaughn posted an .834 OPS and Bauers .873. Versatility or an offseason change is the stronger route.

research.name: Luke Adams
research.assessment: His Triple-A walk and strikeout counts suggest a different profile from the more swing-and-miss-heavy corner bats. The next question is whether that selectivity produces enough damage when MLB pitchers challenge him. A high on-base percentage alone does not create a first-base opening, especially when the incumbent bats have already produced.
research.firstRole: Corner-infield reserve work becomes more plausible if third base is usable. If he is limited to first, a transaction or injury is a much larger part of the opportunity case.
checkpoints: Judge damage on strikes alongside the walk rate, not in place of it.
Follow actual third-base assignments and routine-play reliability.

sourceUpdate.name: Luke Adams
sourceUpdate.finding: A three-homer Triple-A game supplied a power highlight, not proof of sustained MLB-ready impact.

players.name: Jesus Made
players.why: A substantial Double-A sample makes skipping Triple-A plausible. But Turang’s second-base workload and Pratt/Ortiz at short mean that elite prospect status does not create an automatic middle-infield vacancy.
players.opportunity: Third base or an infield reshuffle could open a route if he is defensively ready. That also puts him in competition with Fischer, rather than giving each a separate open position.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports 81% in-zone contact in 2025, alongside inconsistent accuracy on routine throws.
players.checkpoint: Clean up routine throws and footwork; maintain in-zone contact as the pitching improves.
players.monitor: Review routine-play execution and advanced-level contact. The 81% figure is historical scouting data, not a fresh 2026 Prospect Savant measurement.
players.need: Third-base competition is more plausible than a second-base opening: Turang played 151 games there with an .816 OPS. A shortstop route also has competition.

research.name: Jesus Made
research.assessment: A long Double-A season with relatively few strikeouts provides more support for an aggressive promotion than a short hot streak. The distinction is between arm strength and dependable defense: a spectacular throw cannot establish that routine plays are clean. His chance of skipping Triple-A depends on the bat and the available defensive assignment lining up at the same time.
research.firstRole: An infield reshuffle or third-base share is easier to explain than assuming second base opens. A debut could precede an everyday shortstop job.
checkpoints: Keep contact quality as the level improves without giving away swing decisions.
Evaluate routine footwork and throwing accuracy across a run of games.

sourceUpdate.name: Jesus Made

players.name: Sebastian Walcott
players.why: The bat returned strongly after an interrupted season, but the highest-level sample is tiny. Texas has Seager at short, Jung at third and established outfield/DH options; health and defensive fit matter more than the ranking.
players.opportunity: An injury or roster change could create a bat-first route. Outfield work is a possible alternative, not evidence that Texas has promised him an outfield job.
players.observed: FanGraphs’ October report describes his February elbow surgery, July return, mostly DH usage and resumed infield work plus reported outfield drills in the Fall League.
players.checkpoint: Demonstrate healthy, repeatable throws and usable defense at an available position; sustain the bat over a larger advanced-level sample.
players.monitor: Watch defensive workload and throwing recovery. This report does not justify labeling him weak against elevated fastballs.
players.need: No obvious infield vacancy: Seager remains the shortstop and Jung produced an .827 OPS. A healthy bat plus defensive flexibility creates more options.

research.name: Sebastian Walcott
research.assessment: Nine Triple-A plate appearances tell us almost nothing about that level. The more useful questions come from his broader return and the dated scouting report: does the bat continue to produce, and can his throwing support a real defensive home? DH production and defensive readiness must be kept separate after an elbow interruption.
research.firstRole: A bat-first opportunity needs somewhere to play. An infield injury or a demonstrated alternative position could help; outfield drills alone are not a job offer.
checkpoints: Follow the number and frequency of defensive innings, not just whether he appears in a lineup.
Use a larger advanced-level sample before treating a short burst as a settled MLB offensive projection.

players.name: Leo De Vries
players.why: His Double-A record supports the talent case. Recovery now comes first; a saved ETA and prospect rank do not establish readiness for normal hitting and throwing.
players.opportunity: After a healthy return and enough game preparation, third-base competition or an infield reshuffle could create a route. Do not assume a spring opening will align with his return.
players.observed: FanGraphs sees broad offensive potential but inconsistent accuracy on deeper shortstop throws, and identifies third base as a possible alternative behind Wilson.
players.checkpoint: Complete a healthy game return, then reassess long-throw accuracy and routine defense at the position that opens.
players.monitor: Compare throwing consistency and position-specific reps alongside advanced-level contact and power. A positional switch remains conditional.
players.need: Third base is worth testing: Muncy posted a .683 OPS, while Wilson holds shortstop. Gelof’s .797 OPS and cross-position usage complicate that route.

research.name: Leo De Vries
research.assessment: His Double-A record supports the talent case, but the shoulder recovery now takes priority over the depth-chart discussion. An old ETA cannot establish readiness to hit and throw after surgery. Once he resumes games, defensive accuracy and the ability to sustain normal work become more informative than comparing his rank with another healthy prospect.
research.firstRole: A later-season infield opportunity is conditional on rehabilitation and subsequent baseball preparation. This is not an Opening Day forecast.
checkpoints: Obtain a dated club recovery update before moving the expected window earlier.
Reassess throwing and game workload after the return rather than carrying pre-injury assumptions forward.

players.name: Caleb Bonemer
players.why: Double-A power makes him relevant, but Chicago’s infield is occupied: Vargas at third, Montgomery at short, Meidroth at second and Murakami at first. Antonacci also logged substantial left-field work.
players.opportunity: A multi-position assignment could help the club fit his bat, if the defense becomes usable. He still has to beat existing options or benefit from a roster change.
players.observed: FanGraphs identifies fastballs up and away, related changeup vulnerability and inconsistent throws as development areas; second base or left field are possible alternatives.
players.checkpoint: Improve contact against upper-away fastballs without selling out against changeups; make reliable throws at his eventual position.
players.monitor: Track those pitch/location groups separately and watch defensive assignments. Overall home-run totals cannot answer either question.
players.need: The infield is occupied and the saved roster also has Peters, Doyle and Acuña covering center. Defensive versatility can broaden his route without creating a vacant starting job.

research.name: Caleb Bonemer
research.assessment: Power gives Chicago a reason to explore ways to fit the bat, and the announced center-field trial makes that exploration concrete. Learning a position is still different from being ready to play it in MLB. The offensive checkpoint remains whether added damage holds up when pitchers challenge the upper-away area and change speeds.
research.firstRole: A multi-position role could be a bridge to more at-bats. Center-field reps add an option; they do not prove he has displaced an established outfielder.
checkpoints: Track actual center-field reads, routes and throwing decisions, not just assignment announcements.
Look for better contact against the specific pitches identified in the older scouting report.

players.name: Charlie Condon
players.why: A full Triple-A season gives him a stronger proximity case than a brief promotion alone. The right-field/corner mix offers a more plausible route than assuming first base is available.
players.need: Beck posted a .552 OPS, while Johnston and Moniak also took corner work. Rumfield’s .843 OPS makes first base a less obvious production hole.
players.opportunity: Win a corner-outfield share with the bat and playable defense. The Triple-A environment can inflate offense, so raw slugging is not a direct MLB forecast.
players.observed: FanGraphs identifies a rigid bat path and trouble recognizing spin despite substantial raw power; its report also notes prior hand/wrist injuries.
players.checkpoint: Recognize breaking balls earlier and keep contact quality against spin while showing a healthy, repeatable swing.
players.monitor: Compare breaking-ball chase/contact and production away from hitter-friendly parks; no fresh pitch-type split is claimed here.

research.name: Charlie Condon
research.assessment: A full Triple-A workload is a meaningful proximity signal. Still, a strong slugging line in that environment cannot answer the specific concern about recognizing spin. The next useful evidence would show whether he can damage mistakes while refusing breaking balls that finish outside the zone, with the same approach away from favorable hitting conditions.
research.firstRole: A corner-outfield share makes more sense than assuming first base is free. A club can test the bat in a partial role before offering everyday work.
checkpoints: Separate park-driven production from contact and swing decisions.
Check whether breaking-ball recognition holds when pitchers stop offering fastballs in predictable counts.

sourceUpdate.name: Charlie Condon
sourceUpdate.finding: Two grand slams highlighted his Triple-A power; that game does not settle his breaking-ball recognition.

players.name: Ralphy Velazquez
players.why: A substantial Triple-A sample and power production give him a route beyond prospect status. Cleveland already has several first-base options, so he must improve that group rather than simply reach the level.
players.need: Manzardo posted a .684 OPS, Lowe .651 and Hoskins .682. That suggests an offensive upgrade opportunity, although it does not remove roster and defensive competition.
players.opportunity: Earn first-base work with the bat; viable corner-outfield defense would add flexibility. DeLauter and Kwan make an outfield starting spot less automatic.
players.observed: FanGraphs describes a sound contact/power foundation at first base; corner-outfield routes and positioning still need work because speed limits the margin for error.
players.checkpoint: Maintain selective two-strike contact against advanced pitching and become reliable enough in a corner to offer a second position.
players.monitor: Track advanced-level contact plus outfield reads and routes; there is no sourced reason here to invent a specific high-fastball weakness.

research.name: Ralphy Velazquez
research.assessment: The Triple-A combination of power and manageable strikeouts makes the offensive case more tangible than raw-power grades alone. But first base demands continued production, and several alternatives already occupy that lane. A second playable position would matter because it could let the club keep his bat without making one irreversible choice at first.
research.firstRole: First-base competition is plausible; occasional corner-outfield work would expand the ways to get him into the lineup. Neither route removes the need to outperform the existing options.
checkpoints: Maintain contact and damage when pitchers change their two-strike approach.
Confirm usable outfield routes over real games before counting that versatility as established.

players.name: Franklin Arias
players.why: His Triple-A sample and low strikeout rate support a genuine readiness watch. Shortstop defense is part of the case, unlike a bat-only prospect needing an immediate power breakthrough.
players.need: Story posted a .622 OPS and Monasterio .666. An offensive upgrade is possible, but roster decisions and incumbents’ defense still determine access.
players.opportunity: Compete at short or demonstrate useful second-base flexibility. Durbin already logged 151 games at third; moving around the infield is not the same as finding an empty job.
players.observed: FanGraphs reports elite contact and polished shortstop defense, with room for added strength/power and better handling of hard-hit grounders.
players.checkpoint: Preserve contact as velocity rises, turn added strength into game damage and handle sharply hit grounders cleanly.
players.monitor: Track contact and damage together at the higher level; do not manufacture a whiff problem in a player whose reported strength is contact.

research.name: Franklin Arias
research.assessment: The Triple-A contact record gives his readiness case a firmer base than a reputation for defense alone. The important development question is whether the extra power can coexist with that contact as pitchers adjust. Boston’s infield alternatives mean a promotion decision still depends on how much offense and defensive reliability he can provide together.
research.firstRole: Shortstop competition or a flexible infield role could get him started. Strong minor-league production does not by itself establish which incumbent the club would move.
checkpoints: Watch whether power remains when opponents attack him with better velocity.
Preserve routine defensive execution as the game speeds up.

players.monitor: Monitor in-zone contact alongside center-field positioning; the report does not identify a specific pitch type as the sole problem.

research.name: Theo Gillen
research.assessment: His Double-A contact and power provide more support than a High-A breakout alone. The unresolved piece is whether the swing remains controlled against more advanced sequencing while his center-field defense develops. If he cannot stay in center, the offensive standard rises and the range of realistic openings narrows.
research.firstRole: An outfield share becomes easier to justify if he can cover center reliably. A direct Double-A jump would require both the bat and that defensive assignment to be ready.
checkpoints: Look for a steadier head and balanced contact against changing speeds.
Review first steps and routes in center rather than equating speed with finished defense.
